description: We are a passionate and innovative team interested in leveraging technology to solve real-world challenges. Our team has skills in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, web development, UI/UX design, hardware and electronics, and presentation and storytelling. We aim to combine creativity, technical knowledge, and teamwork to develop practical, impactful, and user-friendly solutions.

Astronauts choose a point by map tap or coordinates, then review up to eight destinations within 5 km. Sources include NASA Mars Trek imagery and MOLA shaded relief, USGS geology, TES mineral context, SWIM4MIM ice-consistency imagery, Curiosity’s Gale weather feed and NASA Mars Explorer model grids. ARES fetches model wind, dust opacity, pressure and temperatures for the chosen destination, derives wind speed and direction, and displays source and uncertainty notes. It separates rover observations and model estimates.

It compares a shortest-path baseline with an environment-weighted A* route. Wind exposure, a dust-opacity heuristic, MOLA image texture and manually marked obstacle circles can affect ranking. A simulated blockage triggers replanning. A science explorer presents cited Pahrump Hills evidence without applying it to other locations.

ARES is a research prototype, not operational survival guidance. Weather grids are coarse model context, not route-scale forecasts or active storm alerts. MOLA is shaded imagery, not numeric elevation/slope; the Gale DEM is not integrated, and unmarked hazards are not detected. details:
ARES — Marswalk Mission Intelligence System is a browser-based Mars surface-planning prototype created by Team MAXMARS. It brings map exploration, destination screening, environmental context, science evidence, route comparison and contingency planning into one seven-page briefing. An astronaut selects a landing point by tapping the global map or entering coordinates. ARES then displays up to eight nearby candidate destinations within five kilometres for review. No city names or preset coordinates are imposed on the astronaut’s landing-selection process.

On the map page, users can switch eight information layers: satellite imagery, topography, geological formations, mineral context, temperature and environmental conditions, water-ice indicators, terrain hazards and proposed routes. Destination selection triggers requests for NASA Mars Explorer model fields, allowing the displayed conditions to update for the chosen coordinates rather than reuse values from a different point.

ARES combines planetary data with a route-planning method. NASA Mars Trek supplies global MOLA shaded relief and regional Context Camera and HiRISE imagery around Gale Crater. The USGS global geologic map provides broad formation context. NASA Mars Trek’s TES layer adds coarse mineral context, while the SWIM4MIM browse image provides a global indicator related to subsurface water ice. These sources have different scales and coverage, so the interface identifies their provenance and explains when a layer is regional, coarse, or not registered closely enough to sample at a selected point.

Environmental information is presented with its source and limitations. NASA Mars Explorer model grids provide wind-vector components, dust opacity, surface pressure, air temperature and surface temperature. ARES samples the grids at the selected destination and derives wind speed and direction from the model vectors. A separate Curiosity weather feed provides the Gale station summary and an age indicator. Rover observations and model estimates remain distinct in the interface, because a station reading is not a forecast for every point along a traverse.

For route review, ARES calculates a shortest-path baseline and an environment-weighted A* route across a local grid. It compares distance and relative route cost, and explains which available inputs influenced its ranking. Wind exposure, a bounded dust-opacity term, readable MOLA image texture and operator-marked exclusion circles can affect the comparison. A marked obstacle is treated as a hard block, and the contingency drill demonstrates a simulated blocked region followed by route replanning. Operators can inspect destination and route information before continuing through the briefing.

The science explorer focuses on Pahrump Hills, a documented Curiosity investigation area in Gale Crater. It presents cited NASA and HiRISE evidence and regional geological context. This material is attached to the published Pahrump Hills location; ARES does not claim that it proves scientific value at another selected destination. NASA’s proposed Curiosity route up Mount Sharp is included as a planning precedent, not as a human-safe route.

The seven pages guide users from mission overview and map selection through nearby destination screening, weather review, science context, route comparison and contingency planning. It keeps source notes, uncertainty, missing data and a HOLD status visible. It helps a team explore how multiple evidence types can inform a traversal decision while distinguishing measured observations, model outputs, derived values and simulated inputs.

ARES is a prototype for research and demonstration, not operational survival guidance or a certified safety system. Mars Explorer fields are coarse model context, not route-scale forecasts or active dust-storm alerts. MOLA is shaded imagery, not numeric elevation or slope. The regional Gale DEM is not integrated, and unmarked hazards cannot be detected automatically. No validated astronaut suit limits, crew thresholds or mission approval rules are included. Therefore, ARES ranks candidate paths provisionally and does not declare any route safe or authorize an EVA.
